title: Memory: encoding, storage, retrieval
note: Memory has three jobs: encoding gets information in, storage keeps it, and retrieval brings it back. Information moves from brief sensory memory to limited short-term memory to long-term memory. Processing meaning deeply, and linking new facts to what you already know, makes them easier to retrieve.

read.title: Why meaning beats repetition
text: Imagine two students learning the term 'proactive interference.' The first repeats the definition ten times. The second asks what it means, connects it to writing last year's date in January, and explains it in her own words. A week later, the second student is far more likely to remember it.

Craik and Lockhart's levels-of-processing idea explains why. Shallow processing, such as noticing how a word looks or sounds, leaves a weak trace. Deep processing, thinking about meaning and linking new information to what you already know, leaves a richer one. Studies by Craik and Tulving found that words judged for meaning were remembered best.

Elaborative rehearsal also builds retrieval cues. Memory is organized as a network of linked concepts, so a fact with many connections has many paths back to it. Relating material to yourself is especially powerful, a finding called the self-reference effect.

Repetition is not useless. Maintenance rehearsal keeps a phone number alive in short-term memory for a few seconds. But short-term memory holds only a handful of items for about 15 to 30 seconds. Getting information into long-term memory, where capacity is essentially unlimited, works best through meaning.

q.q: Why did the second student remember the term better?
o: She processed its meaning and linked it to what she knew
She studied it later at night
